--- title: "26 · State Uncertainty" subtitle: "Part V — Multiagent Systems" jupyter: python3 execute: echo: false --- ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"} **Executed in:** Python · **Book:** ADM Ch. 26 · **Lecture:** to be added ::: ## Big picture ### Where this chapter fits [Chapter 25](ch25-sequential-problems.qmd)'s agents all saw the state. Here each agent sees only its own **observations**, as in a POMDP ([Chapter 19](../part4/ch19-beliefs.qmd)–[23](../part4/ch23-controller-abstractions.qmd)), while the others act on theirs. The result, a **partially observable Markov game** (POMG), is the most general model in the book: an MDP, a POMDP, a simple game and a Markov game are all special cases. [Chapter 27](ch27-collaborative-agents.qmd) specializes it to agents that share one reward. **The question:** how do we evaluate and find equilibrium policies when no agent sees the state, and no agent sees what the others see or do? The short answer: **give up on beliefs, and work with whole policies (conditional plans or controllers) as the objects that agents choose between.** - A single agent can't keep a useful belief: the state depends on the others' actions, which depend on *their* observations. - **Evaluation** of a joint policy is still exact: a recursion over conditional plans, or a linear solve for controllers. - A POMG with $h$-step plans is a **simple game whose actions are plans**: its Nash equilibria are the POMG's. - **Dynamic programming** grows plans one step at a time and **prunes** plans that are never a best response, which keeps the game small. ```{dot} //| label: fig-ch26-map //| fig-width: 6.17 //| fig-height: 4.72 //| fig-cap: "Map of this chapter. With partial observability, agents choose among whole policies (conditional plans or controllers). Evaluating joint policies turns the POMG into a simple game over plans, whose equilibria are found as in Chapter 24; dynamic programming prunes plans to keep that game small." //| fig-alt: "Diagram. A blue box, POMG (hidden state, private observations), points to Policies (conditional plans, controllers), then to Joint evaluation (recursion or linear solve), then to Game over plans (actions = whole plans). That points to Equilibria (Chapter 24 methods). A gray box, Dynamic programming (expand and prune), points into Game over plans, labeled keeps it small." digraph ch26 { rankdir=TB; bgcolor="#fcfcfb"; pad=0.25; nodesep=0.4; ranksep=0.4; node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="white", color="#c3c2b7", penwidth=1.2, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=13, fontcolor="#0b0b0b", margin="0.12,0.07"]; edge [color="#52514e", penwidth=1.2, arrowsize=0.7, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11, fontcolor="#52514e"]; pomg [label=<POMG
hidden state, private observations>, fillcolor="#cde2fb", color="#2a78d6"]; pol [label=<Policies
conditional plans, controllers>]; ev [label=<Joint evaluation
recursion or linear solve>]; game [label=<Game over plans
actions = whole plans>]; eq [label=<Equilibria
Chapter 24 methods>, fillcolor="#cde2fb", color="#2a78d6"]; dp [label=<Dynamic programming
expand and prune>, fillcolor="#f0efec"]; pomg -> pol -> ev -> game -> eq; { rank=same; game; dp; } dp -> game [label="keeps it small"]; } ``` ### The key ideas at a glance 1. **A POMG** has a hidden state $s$, joint actions $\boldsymbol{a}$, transitions $T(s' \mid s, \boldsymbol{a})$, a joint observation $\boldsymbol{o} = (o^1, \dots, o^k)$ drawn with probability $O(\boldsymbol{o} \mid \boldsymbol{a}, s')$, and a reward $R^i(s, \boldsymbol{a})$ per agent. Agent $i$ sees only $o^i$. 2. **No beliefs.** In a POMDP the agent updates a belief using its own action and observation. In a POMG the state also depends on the others' actions, which depend on observations it never sees. So policies are written as **conditional plans** (a tree of actions, branching on one's own observations) or **controllers** (a graph of nodes), as in Chapters 20 and 23. 3. **Joint evaluation** is exact: follow every agent's plan together through every state and joint observation (a recursion), or solve linear equations over (joint node, state) pairs for controllers. 4. **Equilibria via a game of plans.** Treat each agent's $h$-step plans as its actions and the joint plans' utilities as rewards: a simple game. Its Nash equilibria are the POMG's $h$-step equilibria. But the number of plans grows doubly exponentially with $h$. 5. **Prune what's never a best response.** Build plans one step at a time, and after each step drop any plan that isn't a best response for *any* distribution over the other agent's plans and the state (a linear program). Equilibria survive; the game stays small. ### Vocabulary | Term | Plain meaning | |:---|:---| | POMG (partially observable stochastic game) | A Markov game where each agent sees only its own observations | | Joint observation $\boldsymbol{o}$ | Everyone's observations together; agent $i$ receives $o^i$ | | Conditional plan | A tree: an action, then a subplan for each of one's own observations | | Controller | A finite graph of nodes with actions and observation-labeled edges | | Game over plans | A simple game whose actions are whole conditional plans | | Dominated plan | A plan that is never a best response, whatever the others do and whatever the state | | Volunteer's dilemma | Everyone wants the job done but would rather someone else did it | : Terms used on this page. {#tbl-vocab} ### After this chapter you can - Write down a POMG, and explain why an agent can't simply keep a belief. - Evaluate joint conditional plans by recursion and joint controllers by a linear solve. - Turn $h$-step plans into a simple game, and find its equilibria. - Prune dominated plans with a linear program, and explain why pruning keeps every equilibrium. - Recognize coordination problems (who acts?) that partial observability makes harder. ## Intuition ::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy"} Two parents share night duty with a baby. Neither sees whether the baby is hungry; both hear it cry, but neither knows whether the other has already got up to feed it. Feeding costs parent 1 less effort than parent 2. The best rule for each depends on the other's rule, and each rule is a plan: "if I hear crying, get up; otherwise sleep". ::: We use **the multicaregiver crying baby** (Appendix F.14; [problem gallery](../appendices/f-problems.qmd#multicaregiver)). A baby is sated or hungry; each of two caregivers can feed, sing or ignore it each hour. Either one feeding sates the baby; otherwise a sated baby turns hungry half the time. Both hear the same thing: a hungry baby cries 90% of the time, a sated one never. Both pay 10 per hour of hunger; feeding costs caregiver 1 an extra 2.5 and caregiver 2 an extra 5; singing costs 0.5 and 0.25. Both start believing the baby is hungry with probability 0.5. ### One hour: nobody feeds With one hour to go, feeding can't help: this hour's hunger cost is already set, and there's no next hour. So both ignore, each paying the expected hunger cost of 5. Planning ahead is what makes feeding worthwhile. ### Plans are the actions With two hours, each caregiver has 27 two-step plans: a first action, then an action for each thing they might hear. Every pair of plans has a value for each caregiver, so the whole problem becomes a 27 × 27 simple game. Its pure Nash equilibria (there are 18, many of them differing only on branches that can't happen) give one of two outcomes: **caregiver 1 feeds first** (payoffs −7.5, −5) or **caregiver 2 does** (−5, −10). It's a volunteer's dilemma: each would rather the other get up. See @eq-plan-eval. ### Throw away what's never best Plans grow fast: 2\,187 three-step plans per caregiver, and 14\,348\,907 four-step ones. But most are never a best response. At the last step, feeding and singing only cost effort, so only "ignore" survives. Growing plans one step at a time and pruning at each step left 4 three-step and 32 four-step plans per caregiver. See @eq-dominance-lp. ### Controllers run forever With no deadline, a caregiver can follow a small controller. If caregiver 2 never feeds, caregiver 1's best 2-node controller feeds **every** hour (worth −30\.0): the baby turns hungry half the time, and an hour of hunger (10) costs more than a feed (2.5). Feeding only after crying is worth −47\.6. Against that, caregiver 2's best response is to never feed, which earns −5\.0: the cost of the first hour's hunger, and nothing after. See @eq-controller-eval. ## Formalism ### Partially observable Markov games A POMG (ADM §26.1; E. A. Hansen, D. S. Bernstein and S. Zilberstein, *AAAI*, 2004) has agents $\mathcal{I}$, states $\mathcal{S}$ with initial distribution $b$, joint actions $\boldsymbol{a}$, transitions $T(s' \mid s, \boldsymbol{a})$, joint observations $\boldsymbol{o} \in \mathcal{O}^1 \times \dots \times \mathcal{O}^k$ with probability $O(\boldsymbol{o} \mid \boldsymbol{a}, s')$, and rewards $R^i(s, \boldsymbol{a})$. After acting, agent $i$ receives only $o^i$. It generalizes everything before it: one agent gives a POMDP; observations that reveal the state give a Markov game; a single state gives a repeated simple game. An agent can't maintain a belief, because updating it would need the other agents' actions and observations, which depend on what those agents believe, and so on. So policies are conditional plans or controllers. ### Evaluating joint conditional plans Let $\boldsymbol{\pi} = (\pi^1, \dots, \pi^k)$ be conditional plans, with root actions $\boldsymbol{\pi}()$ and subplans $\boldsymbol{\pi}(\boldsymbol{o}) = (\pi^1(o^1), \dots, \pi^k(o^k))$. Their joint utility from state $s$ is (ADM eqs. 26.1–26.2) ::: {.key-equation data-name="Joint plan evaluation"} $$ U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s) = R\big(s, \boldsymbol{\pi}()\big) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T\big(s' \mid s, \boldsymbol{\pi}()\big) \sum_{\boldsymbol{o}} O\big(\boldsymbol{o} \mid \boldsymbol{\pi}(), s'\big)\, U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}(\boldsymbol{o})}(s') $$ {#eq-plan-eval} ::: and from the initial distribution, $U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(b) = \sum_s b(s)\, U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s)$. **In words.** Take everyone's first action, collect the reward, then for each next state and joint observation, let each agent follow the branch for its own observation. **Term by term.** - $R(s, \boldsymbol{\pi}())$ is the vector of every agent's reward for the joint root action. - $\boldsymbol{\pi}(\boldsymbol{o})$: each agent moves down its own tree using only its own $o^i$. The sum over joint observations accounts for what the *others* see. - A plan with no subplans ends: its value is just the reward. - The recursion visits every joint path through the trees: $(|\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{O}|)^h$ paths for $h$ steps. **Why it holds.** It is Chapter 20's plan evaluation (eq. 20.8), with joint actions and joint observations: given the state and everyone's plan, the future is fully determined in distribution. ### Evaluating joint controllers For controllers with action distributions $\psi^i(a^i \mid x^i)$ and successor distributions $\eta^i(x^{i\prime} \mid x^i, a^i, o^i)$, the value of joint node $\boldsymbol{x}$ in state $s$ is (ADM eq. 26.3) ::: {.key-equation data-name="Joint controller evaluation"} $$ \begin{aligned} U(\boldsymbol{x}, s) = \sum_{\boldsymbol{a}} \prod_i \psi^i(a^i \mid x^i) \Big[ R(s, \boldsymbol{a}) &+ \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, \boldsymbol{a}) \sum_{\boldsymbol{o}} O(\boldsymbol{o} \mid \boldsymbol{a}, s') \\ &\times \sum_{\boldsymbol{x}'} \prod_i \eta^i(x^{i\prime} \mid x^i, a^i, o^i)\, U(\boldsymbol{x}', s') \Big] \end{aligned} $$ {#eq-controller-eval} ::: **In words.** Chapter 23's controller evaluation, with everyone's nodes moving together. **Term by term.** - The products over $i$ say that agents choose actions and move nodes independently, each on its own observation. - There are $|\mathcal{S}| \prod_i |X^i|$ unknowns: $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$ for two 2-node controllers here. - $U(\boldsymbol{x}, b) = \sum_s b(s) U(\boldsymbol{x}, s)$ gives the value from the initial distribution. **Why it holds.** The joint node and the state together form a Markov chain, as in Chapter 23, so this is its Bellman expectation equation: one linear solve. ### Nash equilibria as a game over plans Build a simple game (ADM §26.3) whose actions for agent $i$ are its $h$-step plans $\Pi^i$ and whose rewards are $U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}, i}(b)$ from @eq-plan-eval. A Nash equilibrium of this game, in pure or mixed plans, is an $h$-step Nash equilibrium of the POMG. The catch is size: with $|\mathcal{A}|$ actions and $|\mathcal{O}|$ observations, $|\Pi_h| = |\mathcal{A}|\,|\Pi_{h-1}|^{|\mathcal{O}|}$. For the caregivers that is 3, 27, 2\,187 and 14\,348\,907 plans for $h = 1, \dots, 4$. ### Dynamic programming with pruning Grow plans one step at a time (ADM §26.4): the $h$-step plans are a first action followed by surviving $(h-1)$-step plans. After each step, drop any plan that is never a best response. Plan $\pi^i$ survives only if some distribution $b(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}, s)$ over the other agents' plans and the state makes it at least as good as every alternative: ::: {.key-equation data-name="Pruning linear program"} $$ \begin{aligned} \max_{\delta,\, b \ge 0}\ \ & \delta \\ \text{s.t.}\ \ & \textstyle\sum_{\boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}, s} b(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}, s) = 1 \\ & \textstyle\sum_{\boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}, s} b(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}, s)\big(U^{\pi^i, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}, i}(s) - U^{\pi^{i\prime}, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}, i}(s)\big) \ge \delta \ \ \text{for all } \pi^{i\prime} \end{aligned} $$ {#eq-dominance-lp} ::: **In words.** Look for a situation, meaning a mix of what the others might do and what the state might be, in which this plan is at least as good as every other. If there's none (the best $\delta$ is negative), prune it. **Term by term.** - $b(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}, s)$: a distribution over the others' plans and the state, playing the role of a belief. No agent computes it; the LP searches over all of them. - $\delta$: the plan's smallest margin over the alternatives, under $b$. Maximizing it finds the most favorable situation. - It's Chapter 20's alpha-vector pruning LP (eq. 20.16), with "state" replaced by "state and the others' plan". **Why it holds.** A plan that is never a best response can't be used in any Nash equilibrium: an agent would switch away from it whatever the others do. Removing it never removes an equilibrium, and every equilibrium of the pruned game is one of the full game. Pruning is repeated over agents until nothing changes, since removing one agent's plans can make more of the other's prunable. ## Worked example ### Two hours with the baby Take caregiver 1's plan "feed now; then ignore whatever you hear" and caregiver 2's plan "ignore twice". Starting 50–50: - **Hour 1.** Caregiver 1 pays 2.5 for feeding; both pay 10 if the baby is hungry now (probability 0.5). Rewards: caregiver 1 $-2.5 - 5 = -7.5$, caregiver 2 $-5$. - **Hour 2.** The feed sated the baby, so it can't be hungry and never cries; both ignore, paying nothing. So the plan pair is worth $(-7.5, -5)$. Can caregiver 1 do better alone? Ignoring twice would leave the baby hungry in hour 2 with probability $0.5 + 0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.75$, costing $-5 + 0.9 \times 0.75 \times (-10) = -11.75$. Any plan that feeds in hour 2 only adds cost, since the game ends after hour 2 and feeding then helps no one. And caregiver 2 is paying nothing extra, so it can't gain either. It's an equilibrium, one of the two outcomes found by brute force above. The code: (−7.500, −5.000) for the pair, and −11.750 for caregiver 1 if it ignores twice instead. ### Is "sing, then ignore" ever worth it? For caregiver 1 at the last step, compare singing, feeding and ignoring for any belief over the state and the other's plan: singing costs 0.5 and feeding 2.5 more than ignoring, and none changes the reward of this hour. So in @eq-dominance-lp, $\delta$ for "sing" is at most $-0.5$ whatever $b$ is. Pruned. That's why the one-step plans shrink from 3 to 1 for each caregiver. ## Interactive ### The three-step game over plans After pruning, each caregiver has 4 three-step plans. Pick one for each, and see what each earns and whether either would switch. Plans are written action[cry: …; quiet: …] with F = feed, S = sing, I = ignore. ```{ojs} planData = FileAttachment("data/ch26-plans.json").json() viewof plan1 = Inputs.select(planData.plans1.map((p, k) => k), {label: "Caregiver 1", format: k => planData.plans1[k]}) viewof plan2 = Inputs.select(planData.plans2.map((p, k) => k), {label: "Caregiver 2", format: k => planData.plans2[k]}) ``` ```{ojs} planNow = { const r1 = planData.R1[plan1][plan2], r2 = planData.R2[plan1][plan2]; const best1 = d3.max(planData.R1, row => row[plan2]), best2 = d3.max(planData.R2[plan1]); return {r1, r2, gain1: best1 - r1, gain2: best2 - r2}; } md`Caregiver 1 earns **${planNow.r1.toFixed(3)}**, caregiver 2 **${planNow.r2.toFixed(3)}**. ${planNow.gain1 < 1e-9 && planNow.gain2 < 1e-9 ? "**A Nash equilibrium:** neither can gain by switching plans." : `Caregiver 1 could gain **${planNow.gain1.toFixed(3)}** by switching, caregiver 2 **${planNow.gain2.toFixed(3)}**.`}` ``` ```{ojs} //| label: fig-plan-explorer //| fig-cap: "The pruned three-step game: caregiver 1's expected reward (left) and caregiver 2's (right) for every pair of surviving plans. The chosen pair is outlined." //| fig-alt: "Two heatmaps, each with caregiver 1's four plans as rows and caregiver 2's four plans as columns; darker cells are worse. An outline marks the chosen pair of plans." { const cells = (R) => R.flatMap((row, i) => row.map((v, j) => ({i, j, v}))); const panel = (R, title) => Plot.plot({ width: 300, height: 260, marginLeft: 40, style: {background: "#fcfcfb"}, title, x: {label: "caregiver 2's plan", tickFormat: d => d + 1}, y: {label: "caregiver 1's plan", tickFormat: d => d + 1}, color: {scheme: "blues", reverse: false, legend: false}, marks: [Plot.cell(cells(R), {x: "j", y: "i", fill: "v"}), Plot.text(cells(R), {x: "j", y: "i", text: d => d.v.toFixed(2), fill: "#0b0b0b", fontSize: 10}), Plot.cell([{i: plan1, j: plan2}], {x: "j", y: "i", fill: "none", stroke: "#eb6834", strokeWidth: 3})]}); return html`
${panel(planData.R1, "Caregiver 1")}${panel(planData.R2, "Caregiver 2")}
`; } ``` ## Algorithms & code ### Plans, evaluation, pruning and controllers ::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"} ## Python ```python def all_plans(n_actions, n_obs, horizon) -> list: """Every conditional plan of the given horizon: an action, then a (horizon - 1)-step plan for each observation.""" plans = [(a,) for a in range(n_actions)] for _ in range(horizon - 1): plans = expand(plans, n_actions, n_obs) return plans def expand(plans, n_actions, n_obs) -> list: """All plans one step longer: any first action, then any plan from `plans` after each observation (|A| |plans|^|O| of them).""" return [(a, subs) for a in range(n_actions) for subs in product(plans, repeat=n_obs)] def plan_evaluator(game): """Returns U(p1, p2, s): both agents' utilities when they follow plans p1 and p2 from state s (eq. 26.1), cached across calls.""" nS = game.T.shape[0] @lru_cache(maxsize=None) def U(p1, p2, s) -> tuple: a1, a2 = p1[0], p2[0] r = game.R[:, s, a1, a2].copy() if len(p1) == 1: # last step: reward only return tuple(r) n1, n2 = game.O.shape[3:] for s2 in range(nS): p = game.T[s, a1, a2, s2] if p == 0: continue for o1 in range(n1): for o2 in range(n2): q = game.O[a1, a2, s2, o1, o2] if q > 0: # each agent follows its own branch sub = U(p1[1][o1], p2[1][o2], s2) r += game.gamma * p * q * np.array(sub) return tuple(r) return U def utility(U, b, p1, p2) -> Array: """eq. 26.2: both agents' utilities from the state distribution b.""" return sum(b[s] * np.array(U(p1, p2, s)) for s in range(len(b))) def plan_game(game, b, plans1, plans2, U=None) -> SimpleGame: """§26.3: the simple game whose actions are whole conditional plans and whose rewards are their utilities from b.""" U = plan_evaluator(game) if U is None else U R = np.zeros((2, len(plans1), len(plans2))) for k1, p1 in enumerate(plans1): for k2, p2 in enumerate(plans2): R[:, k1, k2] = utility(U, b, p1, p2) labels = (tuple(map(str, plans1)), tuple(map(str, plans2))) return SimpleGame(R, labels) def pure_equilibria(g) -> list: """Every pure Nash equilibrium of a two-player simple game: each row is a best response to its column and vice versa (ties allowed).""" A, B = g.R best1 = A >= A.max(axis=0, keepdims=True) - 1e-9 # agent 1 can't gain best2 = B >= B.max(axis=1, keepdims=True) - 1e-9 # agent 2 can't gain return [tuple(map(int, k)) for k in np.argwhere(best1 & best2)] def is_dominated(game, plans, i, k, U) -> bool: """eq. 26.6: is agent i's plan plans[i][k] dominated? Look for a distribution over (the other's plan, state) under which plan k beats every alternative by delta; if the best delta is negative, no such distribution exists, and the plan can go.""" mine, theirs = plans[i], plans[1 - i] nS = game.T.shape[0] def u(pi, pj, s): # agent i's value, either role return U(pi, pj, s)[0] if i == 0 else U(pj, pi, s)[1] # Variables: b over (other plan, state) pairs, then delta. pairs = [(pj, s) for pj in theirs for s in range(nS)] n = len(pairs) rows = [] for alt in mine: if alt == mine[k]: continue # delta - sum_b b (u(k) - u(alt)) <= 0 diff = [u(mine[k], pj, s) - u(alt, pj, s) for pj, s in pairs] rows.append(np.concatenate([-np.array(diff), [1.0]])) if not rows: return False res = linprog(np.concatenate([np.zeros(n), [-1.0]]), # maximize delta A_ub=np.array(rows), b_ub=np.zeros(len(rows)), A_eq=np.concatenate([np.ones(n), [0.0]])[None, :], b_eq=[1.0], bounds=[(0, None)] * n + [(None, None)], method="highs") return -res.fun < -1e-9 # the best delta is negative def prune_dominated(game, plans, U, rng) -> list: """Remove dominated plans, agent by agent in random order, until a full pass removes nothing (§26.4).""" plans = [list(p) for p in plans] changed = True while changed: changed = False for i in rng.permutation(2): for k in rng.permutation(len(plans[i])): if len(plans[i]) > 1 and is_dominated(game, plans, i, k, U): del plans[i][k] changed = True break return plans def dynamic_programming(game, horizon, rng, U=None): """Algorithm 26.4's loop: start from one-step plans; expand and prune, horizon - 1 times. Returns the surviving plans and, for each horizon, how many plans each agent had before and after pruning.""" U = plan_evaluator(game) if U is None else U nA = game.T.shape[1:3] nO = game.O.shape[3:] plans = [[(a,) for a in range(nA[i])] for i in range(2)] plans = prune_dominated(game, plans, U, rng) counts = [(tuple(nA), tuple(map(len, plans)))] for _ in range(horizon - 1): grown = [expand(plans[i], nA[i], nO[i]) for i in range(2)] plans = prune_dominated(game, grown, U, rng) counts.append((tuple(map(len, grown)), tuple(map(len, plans)))) return plans, counts def evaluate_controllers(game, c1, c2) -> Array: """eq. 26.3 by one linear solve. Each controller is (psi, eta) with psi[x, a] and eta[x, a, o, x2], as in Ch. 23. Returns U[x1, x2, s]: the joint value of each pair of nodes in each state.""" (psi1, eta1), (psi2, eta2) = c1, c2 n1, n2, nS = len(psi1), len(psi2), game.T.shape[0] idx = lambda x1, x2, s: (x1 * n2 + x2) * nS + s # flatten (x1, x2, s) m = n1 * n2 * nS M, r = np.eye(m), np.zeros((2, m)) for x1, x2, s in product(range(n1), range(n2), range(nS)): i = idx(x1, x2, s) for a1, a2 in product(range(psi1.shape[1]), range(psi2.shape[1])): w = psi1[x1, a1] * psi2[x2, a2] # both act independently if w == 0: continue r[:, i] += w * game.R[:, s, a1, a2] for s2, o1, o2 in product(range(nS), *map(range, game.O.shape[3:])): p = w * game.T[s, a1, a2, s2] * game.O[a1, a2, s2, o1, o2] if p == 0: continue # Each agent moves its own node on its own observation. nxt = np.outer(eta1[x1, a1, o1], eta2[x2, a2, o2]) for y1, y2 in zip(*np.nonzero(nxt)): M[i, idx(y1, y2, s2)] -= game.gamma * p * nxt[y1, y2] U = np.linalg.solve(M, r.T).T return U.reshape(2, n1, n2, nS) ``` ## Julia ```{.julia .snippet} using ADM g = multicaregiver() # T[s, a1, a2, s′], O[a1, a2, s′, o1, o2], R[i, s, a1, a2] b = [0.5, 0.5] # A plan is (a,) at the last step, or (a, (plan after crying, plan after quiet)). function plans(h) h == 1 && return [(a,) for a in 1:3] return [(a, (p, q)) for a in 1:3 for p in plans(h - 1) for q in plans(h - 1)] end # eq. 26.1: both agents' utilities when following plans p1 and p2 from state s. function evaluate(g, p1, p2, s) a1, a2 = p1[1], p2[1] u = g.R[:, s, a1, a2] length(p1) == 1 && return u for s′ in 1:2, o1 in 1:2, o2 in 1:2 w = g.T[s, a1, a2, s′] * g.O[a1, a2, s′, o1, o2] # Each agent takes the branch for its own observation. w > 0 && (u = u .+ g.γ * w .* evaluate(g, p1[2][o1], p2[2][o2], s′)) end return u end utility(g, p1, p2) = sum(b[s] * evaluate(g, p1, p2, s) for s in 1:2) # The two-step game over plans, and its pure Nash equilibria by brute force. Π = plans(2) Ugame = [utility(g, p1, p2) for p1 in Π, p2 in Π] # Ugame[k1, k2] = [u1, u2] isnash(k1, k2) = all(Ugame[j, k2][1] <= Ugame[k1, k2][1] + 1e-9 for j in eachindex(Π)) && all(Ugame[k1, j][2] <= Ugame[k1, k2][2] + 1e-9 for j in eachindex(Π)) payoffs = unique([round.(Ugame[k1, k2]; digits = 4) for k1 in eachindex(Π), k2 in eachindex(Π) if isnash(k1, k2)]) println(length(Π), " plans each; equilibrium payoffs: ", payoffs) @assert sort(payoffs) == [[-7.5, -5.0], [-5.0, -10.0]] ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Reading the Python code"} - **Plans as nested tuples.** `(0, ((2,), (2,)))` means "feed, then ignore after crying, ignore after quiet". Tuples are hashable, so `functools.lru_cache` can remember each (plan, plan, state) value and reuse it whenever the same subplans meet again. - **`product(plans, repeat=n_obs)`** gives every way to assign a subplan to each observation. - **The pruning LP** puts $\delta$ last among the variables; `linprog` minimizes, so the objective is $-\delta$, and the "at least $\delta$" constraints are rewritten as $\delta - (\dots) \le 0$. - **`evaluate_controllers`** flattens (node 1, node 2, state) into one index and fills the matrix $I - \gamma T$ entry by entry. ::: ### Run them ::: {#03ba82ad .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} game = multicaregiver() plans, counts = P.dynamic_programming(game, 3, np.random.default_rng(0)) for h, (grown, kept) in enumerate(counts, start=1): print(f"horizon {h}: {grown} candidate plans, {kept} kept") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` horizon 1: (3, 3) candidate plans, (1, 1) kept horizon 2: (3, 3) candidate plans, (2, 2) kept horizon 3: (12, 12) candidate plans, (4, 4) kept ``` ::: ::: ### Results #### How many plans survive ::: {#cell-fig-counts .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Plans per caregiver by horizon: all conditional plans (gray), the candidates dynamic programming builds from the previous step's survivors (light blue), and those that survive pruning (blue). So (always feed, never feed) is an equilibrium among 2-node controllers, and a lopsided one. ## Solved problems **Problem 1: special cases.** Show that a POMDP and a Markov game are both POMGs. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"} A POMDP is a POMG with one agent: its observations are the joint observations. A Markov game is a POMG whose observations reveal the state: $\mathcal{O}^i = \mathcal{S}$ and $O(\boldsymbol{o} \mid \boldsymbol{a}, s') = 1$ when every $o^i = s'$. With both, and one agent, it's an MDP. ::: **Problem 2: counting plans.** Each of two agents has 2 actions and 3 observations. How many 1-, 2- and 3-step conditional plans does each have? How many joint plans at 3 steps? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"} $|\Pi_1| = 2$; $|\Pi_2| = 2 \times 2^3 = 16$; $|\Pi_3| = 2 \times 16^3 = 8192$. Joint plans at 3 steps: $8192^2 \approx 6.7 \times 10^7$, each needing an evaluation over every state and joint observation path. That is why pruning is essential. ::: **Problem 3: evaluate a joint plan.** For the caregivers, starting 50–50: caregiver 1 ignores then ignores; caregiver 2 ignores then ignores. What does each earn over two hours? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"} Hour 1: both pay 10 with probability 0.5: $-5$ each. With nobody feeding, the baby is hungry in hour 2 with probability $0.5 \times 1 + 0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.75$, costing $0.9 \times 0.75 \times 10 = 6.75$. Each earns $-11.75$. Either caregiver could improve by feeding in hour 1, which makes this plan pair not an equilibrium. ::: **Problem 4: prune by hand.** At the last step, caregiver 2's options are feed (extra −5), sing (−0.25) and ignore (0), and none affects this step's hunger cost. Write the pruning LP for "sing", and solve it. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"} For any distribution $b$ over caregiver 1's plan and the state, "sing" minus "ignore" is $-0.25$ exactly (hunger costs cancel). The constraint against "ignore" is $-0.25 \ge \delta$, so $\delta \le -0.25 < 0$: "sing" is dominated and pruned. "Feed" is pruned the same way, with $\delta \le -5$. ::: **Problem 5: why can't caregiver 1 keep a belief?** Caregiver 1 hears "quiet" after ignoring. Why can't it update $P(\text{hungry})$ with the Chapter 19 filter? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"} The filter needs the transition model for the action taken, and here the transition depends on the *joint* action: if caregiver 2 fed, the baby is certainly sated. Caregiver 1 doesn't see whether caregiver 2 fed. It could average over caregiver 2's policy, but that policy depends on what caregiver 2 heard and believes, which depends on caregiver 1's policy, and so on. Committing to whole plans or controllers sidesteps the regress: every agent's behavior is fixed in advance, and evaluation averages over everything. ::: ## Recap 1. **A POMG is the most general model in the book (@eq-plan-eval).** *Why it matters:* MDPs, POMDPs, simple games and Markov games are all special cases; the difficulty comes from each agent seeing only part of the picture. 2. **Without shared information, agents choose whole policies instead of acting on beliefs.** *Why it matters:* conditional plans and controllers (Chapters 20, 23) become the objects of the game, and their evaluation stays exact. 3. **A POMG over $h$-step plans is a simple game over plans.** *Why it matters:* Chapter 24's equilibrium methods apply directly, but the number of plans explodes: 14\,348\,907 four-step plans per caregiver. 4. **Pruning never-best plans keeps the game small without losing equilibria (@eq-dominance-lp).** *Why it matters:* for the caregivers, 32 plans survive at four steps; the same idea drives Chapter 27's methods for cooperative teams. 5. **Coordination is the hard part.** *Why it matters:* the caregivers' equilibria are all "one works, the other free-rides" or worse; partial observability makes it harder to share the work, which is what shared rewards (Chapter 27) change. ## Cheat sheet & connections | Name | Formula | Ref | |---|---|---| | Joint plan evaluation | $U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s) = R(s, \boldsymbol{\pi}()) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T \sum_{\boldsymbol{o}} O\, U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}(\boldsymbol{o})}(s')$ | @eq-plan-eval | | Joint controller evaluation | $U(\boldsymbol{x}, s) = \sum_{\boldsymbol{a}} \prod_i \psi^i [R + \gamma \sum T \sum O \sum_{\boldsymbol{x}'} \prod_i \eta^i\, U(\boldsymbol{x}', s')]$ | @eq-controller-eval | | Game over plans | actions $\Pi^i_h$, rewards $U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}, i}(b)$ | §26.3 | | Pruning LP | $\max \delta$: some $b(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}, s)$ makes $\pi^i$ beat every alternative by $\delta$ | @eq-dominance-lp | : Key equations from this page. {#tbl-cheatsheet} **Common pitfalls** - **Letting an agent use information it doesn't have.** Plans branch only on the agent's own observations, never on the others' or on the state. - **Enumerating plans naively.** Their number is doubly exponential in the horizon; grow and prune instead. - **Counting equivalent plans as different equilibria.** Plans that differ only on impossible branches earn the same; the page reports distinct payoffs. - **Forgetting that pruning must repeat.** Removing one agent's plans can make more of the other's prunable. **Connections** - [Ch 20 · Exact Belief State Planning](../part4/ch20-exact-belief-state-planning.qmd): conditional plans and the alpha-vector pruning LP. - [Ch 23 · Controller Abstractions](../part4/ch23-controller-abstractions.qmd): controllers and their evaluation. - [Ch 24 · Multiagent Reasoning](ch24-multiagent-reasoning.qmd): equilibria of the game over plans. - [Ch 25 · Sequential Problems](ch25-sequential-problems.qmd): the fully observed version. - [Ch 27 · Collaborative Agents](ch27-collaborative-agents.qmd): the same models when all agents share one reward.
